screens.title: How mongos routes queries and updates
screens.narratorSegment: mongos is a lightweight routing process that consults cluster metadata to decide where to send an operation. The core claim is simple: when a query predicate includes the shard key in a form mongos can resolve, mongos routes to the shard or shards owning matching chunks. If the predicate lacks shard key information, mongos cannot infer a single owner and issues the operation to every shard — a scatter-gather. A concrete example: with a products collection sharded by {category: 1, productId: 1}, a find that includes both category and productId can be routed to one shard because the chunk map pinpoints the owning chunk. A contrast: a query by price alone lacks the shard key so mongos queries all shards and merges results, which increases network traffic and C P U at the router. A common misconception is that adding an index on the queried field removes the need for shard key information; indexes speed local shard scans but do not change routing. Key takeaway: design predicates so mongos can use the shard key to avoid scatter-gather costs. How could you rewrite an existing query to include the shard key and achieve a targeted route?

keyIdea.title: Routing principle
keyIdea.text: mongos uses shard key values in predicates to target specific shards; otherwise it must scatter-gather across all shards.

content.html:
Core Concept

mongos routing behavior

mongos consults the cluster metadata to determine which shard owns the chunk for a given shard key value. If it can identify owners, the operation is sent only to those shards.

Definition
Targeted routing: predicate contains shard key value(s) so mongos knows the shard owner.
Practical example
With shard key {"category", "productId"}, the filter {"category":"Electronics","productId":"P001"} is targeted to one shard.
Misconception
An index on a non-shard field speeds local scans but does not allow mongos to avoid scatter-gather routing.
Annotated flow
Step 1 — Receive query
Application sends filter to mongos.
Step 2 — Consult metadata
mongos looks up the shard key ranges on the config servers.
Step 3 — Target or broadcast
If shard key present, target; otherwise broadcast to all shards for scatter-gather.
Key takeaway
Shard key presence controls routing. Plan filters accordingly to reduce cross-shard work.

screens.title: Targeted Queries
screens.narratorSegment: A targeted query includes the full shard key or a compound key prefix in a form that mongos can resolve to a shard or a subset of shards. Concretely, if a collection is sharded by {"category":1, "productId":1}, a filter such as {"category":"Electronics","productId":"P001"} is targeted because it supplies both shard key fields. A slightly different case: {"category":"Electronics"} supplies a prefix of the compound key and can be routed to shards that hold that category. Targeted queries minimize network traffic because only relevant shards are asked to perform work and return results. Example: an e-commerce A P I that fetches a single product by category and productId will be fast and consistent when the query is targeted. A common misconception is that loose match patterns like range queries against a hashed shard key will be targeted; they are not. Key takeaway: when you can include shard key fields in application filters, prefer that pattern to reduce latency and mongos C P U usage. Consider whether your read paths can be rewritten to add shard key values or prefixes. Targeted Queries means include full shard key or compound prefix values to allow mongos to route to the minimal set of shards.. In practical terms, what makes a query targeted and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Targeted Query rule
keyIdea.text: Include full shard key or compound prefix values to allow mongos to route to the minimal set of shards.

content.html:
Definition

Targeted Queries

A query that provides shard key values so mongos can pinpoint the owning shard(s).

Concrete example
db.products.find({ "category": "Electronics", "productId": "P001" })
This will be routed to the single shard that contains that chunk range for category and productId.
Why it matters
Reduces network calls and processing, and yields lower latency for point lookups.
Misconception
Adding indexes on the query field alone does not change routing; mongos still needs shard key values to target.
Rewrite pattern
If your API receives productId and category separately, build the filter to include both before calling the database. When only category is known, expect subset routing to matching shards for that category prefix.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Provide shard key values when possible to let mongos route precisely and avoid costly scatter-gather operations.

screens.title: Scatter-Gather Queries
screens.narratorSegment: A scatter-gather query occurs when the query predicate does not contain the shard key or contains it in a way mongos cannot resolve to a single owner. In that situation mongos broadcasts the query to every shard, waits for each shard's partial results, and then merges or sorts them before returning to the client. For example, if your products collection is sharded by category and productId and you query by price only, such as price greater than 500, mongos will query all shards because price is not part of the shard key. This increases network bandwidth, raises C P U usage on mongos as it merges results, and can create unpredictable latency in large clusters. A common mistake is assuming that an index on the queried field eliminates the broadcast; indexes help shard-local performance but do not change routing. When scatter-gather is unavoidable, limit result sizes, paginate carefully, and consider adding shard-key-friendly access patterns or a supporting lookup table that maps query attributes to shard keys. Closing question: where in your application are price-range or attribute-only queries common, and can you restructure the path to include shard key information?

keyIdea.text: Queries that lack shard key information are broadcast to all shards, increasing network and coordination overhead.

content.html:
Definition

Scatter-Gather Queries

When mongos cannot identify a shard owner from the predicate, it sends the query to every shard and merges results.

Concrete example
db.products.find({ "price": { $gt: 500 } })
Because price is not part of the shard key, this will be broadcast to all shards and merged.
Why it hurts
Higher network usage, more CPU on mongos, and longer query tail latency in large clusters.
Mitigation
Consider denormalized lookup tables or storing commonly queried attributes with shard key fields to enable targeted access.
Checklist for scatter-gather
  • Confirm whether the predicate contains the shard key or a usable prefix.
  • Estimate the number of shards and expected per-shard work.
  • Limit result sets, add projection, and apply server-side pagination.
  • Where feasible, add an access pattern mapping to the shard key.
Key Takeaway

Treat attribute-only queries as potential scatter-gather costs and redesign critical paths to include shard key info when performance matters.

screens.title: Updates and Deletes in a Sharded Cluster
screens.narratorSegment: Update and delete operations follow the same routing principle as reads: include the shard key in the query predicate to make them targeted. A targeted update only touches the relevant shard, minimizing coordination and avoiding unnecessary work. For example, updating price with both category and productId in the filter is efficient. In contrast, updateMany that filters by name or other non-shard fields is broadcast to all shards and executed where matching documents exist. The chapter's code examples show both patterns. Another important rule: modifying a document's shard key value is generally disallowed or requires special handling because changing the shard key would imply moving the document between chunks and possibly shards. The common workaround is to delete and re-insert the document with the new shard key, or use collection-wide resharding if appropriate. A common mistake is relying on an untargeted update that coincidentally affects only one shard in development but will be slow or unsafe in production. Key takeaway: write updates and deletes with shard key predicates to ensure they are routed efficiently and avoid in-place shard key changes. Updates and Deletes in a Sharded Cluster means include the shard key in update/delete predicates; avoid modifying shard key values directly to prevent complex cross-shard moves.. In practical terms, how to make updates efficient and the rules when shard keys are involved. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Update rule
keyIdea.text: Include the shard key in update/delete predicates; avoid modifying shard key values directly to prevent complex cross-shard moves.

content.html:
Process Flow

Targeted update example

db.products.updateOne(
  { "category": "Electronics", "productId": "P001" },
  { $set: { "price": 999.99 } }
)
This is targeted and sent to the single shard containing that chunk range.
Untargeted update example
db.products.updateMany(
  { "name": "Laptop XYZ" },
  { $set: { "description": "Updated description" } }
)
This will be broadcast to every shard and applied where matches occur.
Why changing a shard key is problematic

A shard key defines the document's logical placement. Modifying it would require moving the document between chunks and possibly shards, which is complex and typically blocked. The usual approach is to delete and re-insert with the new shard key value or reshard the collection if necessary.

Common mistake
Attempting large untargeted updates that were acceptable in small test clusters but cause heavy load in production.
Key Takeaway

Make updates targeted by including shard keys and never assume modifying shard keys is allowed without additional steps.

screens.title: Modifying Shard Keys: Rules and Workarounds
screens.narratorSegment: Modifying a shard key value in an update is generally disallowed or requires special handling because the shard key determines a document's placement in chunks and on shards. If you were allowed to change the shard key in place, MongoDB would have to move the document to a different chunk and potentially a different shard, which complicates consistency and performance. The practical workaround is straightforward: if you must change the shard key for an object, read and store the document, delete the original, and insert a new document with the new shard key value. Alternatively, if you need to change shard key semantics for many documents, plan a reshard operation for the whole collection. A common misconception is that a single update that modifies the shard key will be automatically and cheaply migrated; it is not. Example scenario: if product ownership moves between categories and category is part of the shard key, you should implement a delete-and-reinsert pattern or design the application to avoid changing shard key attributes. Takeaway: avoid mutable shard keys where possible and design application models that keep shard key values stable.

keyIdea.title: Shard key immutability
keyIdea.text: Shard key values are effectively immutable for safe, efficient operation; change them only via delete+reinsert or collection resharding.

content.html:
Definition

Modifying Shard Keys

Directly changing a shard key value in an update is generally not allowed because it implies relocating the document across chunks and shards.

Safe workaround
Read the existing document, delete it, and insert a new document with the updated shard key. For large-scale changes, plan a reshard operation for the whole collection.
Example scenario

If category is part of the shard key and a product moves from Home to Electronics, don't try to update the category field in place. Instead, copy the document, delete the old one, and insert with the new category value.

Common misconception
Developers sometimes assume the cluster will transparently move documents when shard keys change. It will not do so cheaply; you must perform explicit steps or reshard.
Key Takeaway

Treat shard key fields as effectively immutable. If you must change them, use delete-and-reinsert or reshard the collection.

screens.title: Transactions in Sharded Clusters
screens.narratorSegment: MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions in sharded clusters, but they add coordination overhead because operations may touch multiple shards. The mongos router coordinates the distributed transaction using a session object that groups operations until commit or abort. In practice you create a session, start a transaction, perform updates or inserts on one or more collections across shards, and then commit. A concrete example: decrementing a user's balance and inserting an order in separate collections can be done inside a single transaction if both operations include shard key values to ensure each write is routed efficiently. Transactions guarantee atomicity, but they are generally higher-latency than single-document writes because of two-phase commit-like coordination. A common misconception is to treat transactions as a free replacement for careful schema design; they are powerful but should be short, touch few shards, and avoid modifying shard keys. Key takeaway: use transactions when you need cross-document atomicity, but design them to be brief and targeted to limit coordination cost. keyIdea.title: Transaction principle
keyIdea.text: Transactions provide ACID across shards via session coordination, but expect higher latency and coordination overhead—keep them short and focused.

content.html:
Core Concept

Multi-shard Transactions

Transactions span multiple shards by coordinating operations under a session. mongos acts as the coordinator and ensures atomic commit or abort.

Code example (visual)
const session = db.getMongo().startSession();
session.startTransaction();

try {
  const users = session.getDatabase("myAppDB").collection("users");
  const orders = session.getDatabase("myAppDB").collection("orders");

  users.updateOne({ "userId": "user123", "country": "USA" }, { $inc: { "balance": -50 } }, { session });
  orders.insertOne({ "orderId": "ORD456", "userId": "user123", "country": "USA", "amount": 50 }, { session });

  session.commitTransaction();
} catch (error) {
  session.abortTransaction();
} finally {
  session.endSession();
}
When to use transactions
  • When multi-document atomicity is required across collections or shards.
  • When compensating actions would be error-prone or risky.
  • Avoid for high-throughput hot paths unless necessary, due to latency.
Best practice
Keep transactions short, target operations when possible, and avoid touching many shards.

Use transactions for correctness but expect coordination cost. Design schemas and queries to reduce cross-shard touches within transactions.

screens.title: Transaction Limitations and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Transactions in sharded clusters are powerful but come with trade-offs. The coordinator must communicate with each involved shard and ensure commit consistency, which increases latency and the potential for contention. A best practice is to keep transactions brief and avoid scanning or updating large document sets within a transaction. Where possible, design workflows so that transactional work touches a single shard by including shard key values in the operations. Also avoid modifying shard keys inside a transaction because moving documents between shards during a transaction is complex and error-prone. A practical pattern: perform quick checks and small writes inside the transaction and push heavy data migrations or batch changes to out-of-band jobs. A common misconception is that transactions scale automatically; in reality, many large transactions reduce throughput. Process Flow

Best practices for sharded transactions

Keep transactions short
Short transactions reduce lock time and coordination windows across shards.
Target shards when possible
Include shard key values so operations touch fewer shards during commit.
Avoid shard-key changes
Resharding or delete-and-reinsert is the safer approach for key changes.
Common mistakes
  • Holding open transactions during user input or long processing.
  • Including wide scans or large updates inside a transaction.
  • Assuming transactions remove the need for shard-aware design.
Key Takeaway

Use transactions for correctness where needed, but design them to be as small and targeted as possible to reduce coordination costs.

screens.title: Classify queries for a sharded e-commerce catalog
screens.narratorSegment: Let's work through a hands-on classification exercise using a products collection sharded by {"category":1, "productId":1}. Operation one: find a specific product by both productId and category. This is targeted because the predicate provides the full compound shard key, so mongos can route to a single shard. Operation two: find all products in the Electronics category. This uses a prefix of the shard key and will be targeted to the shards that hold that category range — more shards may be involved depending on chunk distribution, but mongos does not broadcast to all shards unnecessarily. Operation three: find products with price greater than 500. Since price is not part of the shard key, this is a scatter-gather query requiring mongos to query every shard and merge results. Operation four: update price for a product given category and productId. This is a targeted update; it will be routed to the owning shard and be efficient. For each classification, consider whether you can rewrite the query to include shard key values, or add an access layer that maps attributes to shard keys to avoid broadcasts. Which operations in your application can be rewritten to include shard keys?

content.html:
Hands-on Activity

Classify these operations

Operation 1
db.products.find({ "category": "Books", "productId": "B001" })
Classification: Targeted. Reason: full shard key provided; mongos can route to one shard.
Operation 2
db.products.find({ "category": "Electronics" })
Classification: Targeted to shards owning that category range. Reason: prefix of compound shard key is provided.
Operation 3
db.products.find({ "price": { $gt: 500 } })
Classification: Scatter-gather. Reason: price is not part of shard key, so mongos must query all shards.
Operation 4
db.products.updateOne({ "category": "Home & Kitchen", "productId": "H007" }, { $set: { "price": 49.99 } })
Classification: Targeted update. Reason: predicate includes shard key allowing single-shard routing.
Reflection

For each scatter-gather case, ask whether you can add shard key values, denormalize frequently queried attributes with shard key fields, or maintain a mapping table that helps you perform a targeted lookup first.

Key Takeaway

Use these classifications to rewrite critical queries so they become targeted, improving latency and reducing cluster load.

screens.title: Performance: Targeted vs Scatter-Gather
screens.narratorSegment: Comparing targeted and scatter-gather queries helps prioritize engineering effort. Targeted queries hit one shard or a small subset, minimizing network hops and C P U cycles on mongos and shards. Their latency is typically lower and more predictable because only one shard performs the work. Scatter-gather queries broadcast to all shards, increasing network traffic and requiring mongos to merge results, which increases C P U and can cause unpredictable tail latency as the slowest shard determines completion. An example contrast: a point lookup by productId and category is targeted and returns quickly. A range query on a non-shard field, like price, will query all shards and take longer as shard count grows. For best use, design common read and write paths around shard-key-inclusive filters, paginate on targeted result sets, and avoid global scans. Misconception to avoid: adding replicas or indexes alone does not make a scatter-gather query targeted — change the filter shape or the data model instead. Closing prompt: what is the worst-case cost of a scatter-gather on a many-shard cluster and which of your queries risks that cost?

Comparison

Targeted

  • Routes to a specific shard using shard key values.
  • Low network and CPU usage; predictable latency.
  • Ideal for point lookups and writes when shard key is known.
When to use

Design API calls to include shard key values for frequent reads and writes.

Comparison

Scatter-Gather

  • Broadcasts query to all shards when shard key is missing.
  • Higher network traffic and mongos CPU; latency grows with shard count.
  • Use for ad-hoc analytics or when targeted access is impossible.
Mitigation
Add mapping layers, denormalize, or limit scatter-gather queries to off-peak windows.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how queries and updates behave when your data is spread across shards and why the shard key is central to performance. We'll start with how the mongos router decides whether an operation is targeted to a specific shard or must be sent to every shard in a scatter-gather. You will learn practical rules: include the full shard key or an appropriate prefix for efficient targeting, and avoid modifying shard keys in-place. We'll also examine how updates and deletes are routed and when multi-document transactions span multiple shards. Concrete examples use a sharded products collection with a compound shard key of category and productId. By the end you will be able to classify operations as targeted or scatter-gather, choose efficient update patterns, and plan short, targeted transactions when needed. A short checklist and a hands-on activity guide will help you apply these patterns to an e-commerce catalog scenario. Keep in mind: correct shard key usage reduces network traffic, lowers mongos C P U, and often yields orders-of-magnitude improvement in latency compared to scatter-gather operations.

By the end of this chapter you'll distinguish targeted queries from scatter-gather queries and explain why the shard key controls routing. You will analyze how including or omitting a shard key influences latency and resource use, and practice classifying operations on a sharded products collection. You'll understand how update and delete operations behave in a sharded environment, including the constraints when an update attempts to change a shard key. Finally, you'll learn how multi-document transactions work in sharded clusters, their coordination overhead, and practical limits that suggest keeping transactions short and targeted. Each objective combines definition, practical examples, and a quick mnemonic to help you remember when operations will be routed to a single shard. These skills let you design queries and write updates that minimize scatter-gather traffic, reduce mongos C P U usage, and improve overall cluster performance. We'll verify competency with a milestone that asks you to classify four sample operations and justify efficient rewrite strategies.

This second objectives page emphasizes practice and verification. You'll apply classification skills to a products catalog: decide if a find or update is targeted or scatter-gather and rewrite queries to include the shard key when possible. You'll run through a hands-on activity that asks you to write four commands against a collection sharded by category and productId, explain routing, and reason about performance. We'll also walk through an example transaction across two collections, showing how session objects coordinate commits. Finally, you'll learn common mistakes to avoid, such as issuing long-running transactions or attempting to modify shard keys in place. Each objective includes a micro-milestone so you can self-verify: classify operations, write targeted updates, and explain transaction trade-offs. Practicing these actions will make shard-aware application design a habit and reduce costly scatter-gather operations in production systems.

mongos is a lightweight routing process that consults cluster metadata to decide where to send an operation. The core claim is simple: when a query predicate includes the shard key in a form mongos can resolve, mongos routes to the shard or shards owning matching chunks. If the predicate lacks shard key information, mongos cannot infer a single owner and issues the operation to every shard — a scatter-gather. A concrete example: with a products collection sharded by {category: 1, productId: 1}, a find that includes both category and productId can be routed to one shard because the chunk map pinpoints the owning chunk. A contrast: a query by price alone lacks the shard key so mongos queries all shards and merges results, which increases network traffic and C P U at the router. A common misconception is that adding an index on the queried field removes the need for shard key information; indexes speed local shard scans but do not change routing. Key takeaway: design predicates so mongos can use the shard key to avoid scatter-gather costs. How could you rewrite an existing query to include the shard key and achieve a targeted route?

A targeted query includes the full shard key or a compound key prefix in a form that mongos can resolve to a shard or a subset of shards. Concretely, if a collection is sharded by {"category":1, "productId":1}, a filter such as {"category":"Electronics","productId":"P001"} is targeted because it supplies both shard key fields. A slightly different case: {"category":"Electronics"} supplies a prefix of the compound key and can be routed to shards that hold that category. Targeted queries minimize network traffic because only relevant shards are asked to perform work and return results. Example: an e-commerce A P I that fetches a single product by category and productId will be fast and consistent when the query is targeted. A common misconception is that loose match patterns like range queries against a hashed shard key will be targeted; they are not. Key takeaway: when you can include shard key fields in application filters, prefer that pattern to reduce latency and mongos C P U usage. Consider whether your read paths can be rewritten to add shard key values or prefixes. Targeted Queries means include full shard key or compound prefix values to allow mongos to route to the minimal set of shards.. In practical terms, what makes a query targeted and why it matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A scatter-gather query occurs when the query predicate does not contain the shard key or contains it in a way mongos cannot resolve to a single owner. In that situation mongos broadcasts the query to every shard, waits for each shard's partial results, and then merges or sorts them before returning to the client. For example, if your products collection is sharded by category and productId and you query by price only, such as price greater than 500, mongos will query all shards because price is not part of the shard key. This increases network bandwidth, raises C P U usage on mongos as it merges results, and can create unpredictable latency in large clusters. A common mistake is assuming that an index on the queried field eliminates the broadcast; indexes help shard-local performance but do not change routing. When scatter-gather is unavoidable, limit result sizes, paginate carefully, and consider adding shard-key-friendly access patterns or a supporting lookup table that maps query attributes to shard keys. Closing question: where in your application are price-range or attribute-only queries common, and can you restructure the path to include shard key information?

Update and delete operations follow the same routing principle as reads: include the shard key in the query predicate to make them targeted. A targeted update only touches the relevant shard, minimizing coordination and avoiding unnecessary work. For example, updating price with both category and productId in the filter is efficient. In contrast, updateMany that filters by name or other non-shard fields is broadcast to all shards and executed where matching documents exist. The chapter's code examples show both patterns. Another important rule: modifying a document's shard key value is generally disallowed or requires special handling because changing the shard key would imply moving the document between chunks and possibly shards. The common workaround is to delete and re-insert the document with the new shard key, or use collection-wide resharding if appropriate. A common mistake is relying on an untargeted update that coincidentally affects only one shard in development but will be slow or unsafe in production. Key takeaway: write updates and deletes with shard key predicates to ensure they are routed efficiently and avoid in-place shard key changes. Updates and Deletes in a Sharded Cluster means include the shard key in update/delete predicates; avoid modifying shard key values directly to prevent complex cross-shard moves.. In practical terms, how to make updates efficient and the rules when shard keys are involved. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Modifying a shard key value in an update is generally disallowed or requires special handling because the shard key determines a document's placement in chunks and on shards. If you were allowed to change the shard key in place, MongoDB would have to move the document to a different chunk and potentially a different shard, which complicates consistency and performance. The practical workaround is straightforward: if you must change the shard key for an object, read and store the document, delete the original, and insert a new document with the new shard key value. Alternatively, if you need to change shard key semantics for many documents, plan a reshard operation for the whole collection. A common misconception is that a single update that modifies the shard key will be automatically and cheaply migrated; it is not. Example scenario: if product ownership moves between categories and category is part of the shard key, you should implement a delete-and-reinsert pattern or design the application to avoid changing shard key attributes. Takeaway: avoid mutable shard keys where possible and design application models that keep shard key values stable.

MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions in sharded clusters, but they add coordination overhead because operations may touch multiple shards. The mongos router coordinates the distributed transaction using a session object that groups operations until commit or abort. In practice you create a session, start a transaction, perform updates or inserts on one or more collections across shards, and then commit. A concrete example: decrementing a user's balance and inserting an order in separate collections can be done inside a single transaction if both operations include shard key values to ensure each write is routed efficiently. Transactions guarantee atomicity, but they are generally higher-latency than single-document writes because of two-phase commit-like coordination. Let's work through a hands-on classification exercise using a products collection sharded by {"category":1, "productId":1}. Operation one: find a specific product by both productId and category. This is targeted because the predicate provides the full compound shard key, so mongos can route to a single shard. Operation two: find all products in the Electronics category. This uses a prefix of the shard key and will be targeted to the shards that hold that category range — more shards may be involved depending on chunk distribution, but mongos does not broadcast to all shards unnecessarily. Operation three: find products with price greater than 500. Since price is not part of the shard key, this is a scatter-gather query requiring mongos to query every shard and merge results. Operation four: update price for a product given category and productId. This is a targeted update; it will be routed to the owning shard and be efficient. For each classification, consider whether you can rewrite the query to include shard key values, or add an access layer that maps attributes to shard keys to avoid broadcasts. Which operations in your application can be rewritten to include shard keys?

Comparing targeted and scatter-gather queries helps prioritize engineering effort. Targeted queries hit one shard or a small subset, minimizing network hops and C P U cycles on mongos and shards. Their latency is typically lower and more predictable because only one shard performs the work. Scatter-gather queries broadcast to all shards, increasing network traffic and requiring mongos to merge results, which increases C P U and can cause unpredictable tail latency as the slowest shard determines completion. An example contrast: a point lookup by productId and category is targeted and returns quickly. A range query on a non-shard field, like price, will query all shards and take longer as shard count grows. For best use, design common read and write paths around shard-key-inclusive filters, paginate on targeted result sets, and avoid global scans. Misconception to avoid: adding replicas or indexes alone does not make a scatter-gather query targeted — change the filter shape or the data model instead. Use this checklist to audit and optimize your application for sharded clusters. First, verify whether critical read and write paths include the shard key or a usable prefix. If not, determine whether you can change the A P I, denormalize data, or add a small mapping collection to translate common query attributes into shard key values. Second, for update and delete operations, require shard key predicates in code paths that must be efficient; treat untargeted updateMany calls as high-risk. Third, avoid modifying shard keys in-place; use delete-and-reinsert or resharding for bulk changes. Fourth, keep multi-document transactions short and target them to a small number of shards. Fifth, instrument mongos and shards to observe scatter-gather frequency and long-tail latencies, then prioritize rewriting the most frequent broad queries. A common oversight is applying fixes to one endpoint while other services still issue scatter-gather queries. Key takeaway: iterate on this checklist and measure results after each change to ensure performance gains. Here are three core concepts to carry forward. First, a targeted query includes the shard key or an appropriate prefix so mongos can route to the owning shard(s); this is the most efficient pattern for reads and writes. Second, a scatter-gather query lacks shard key routing information and is broadcast to all shards, which increases network and C P U usage and makes latency less predictable. Third, updates and deletes should include shard key predicates to be targeted; attempts to modify shard key values are disallowed or require delete-and-reinsert semantics. Keep these three ideas in mind when you design your APIs and schema: prefer shard-key-aware access, avoid in-place shard key mutations, and treat scatter-gather queries as a performance cost to minimize.
